To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
intracellular AbetaPP is detected in all subjects, independent of disease state, with antibodies that recognize Abeta and AbetaPP, but not with antibodies that recognize neoepitopes.
the intracellular AbetaPP immunoreactivity is detected in the human brain independent of age, disease state, or the existence of extracellular amyloid plaques.
the intracellular accumulation is AbetaPP and not Abeta, and that the staining results vary depending on the chosen pretreatment strategy and the antibody used.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the detection of AbetaPP or Abeta in the intracellular space and the results suggest that the detection of intracellular AbbetaPP and Abeta may depend on the antibodies used, the age, and the disease state of the subjects.
a critical evaluation of the use of AbetaPP antibodies in immunohistochemistry and with the presence of AbbetaPP and Abeta in extra- and the intracellular compartment in human brain tissue samples.
the intracellular localization of AbetaPP, and the presence of Abbeta.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

intracellular accumulation of immunoreactivity for AbetaPP and/or Abeta cannot be excluded in human brain tissue, but that this accumulation cannot be confirmed with the antibodies and pretreatment strategies used in the present study.
AbetaPP is present intracellularly in all subjects independent of age or disease state.
AbetaPP is present in the intracellular compartments in all age groups, while intracellular Abeta can be detected only in Alzheimer's disease subjects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the immunohistochemical visualization is a useful method for detecting intracellular AbetaPP and that the presence of intracelullar AbetaPP is not specific for AD.
AbetaPP is detected intracellular in all age groups and with all antibodies tested, whereas Abeta is detected intracellular with some antibodies in subjects with AD.

intracellular accumulation of amyloid-beta (Ab) is not a general phenomenon in human brain, but is dependent on the antibody used, the pretreatment of the sample, and the disease state of the subject.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is AbetAPP rather than Abeta which accumulates in the intracellular compartments in human brains.
it is important to use different antibodies and pretreatment strategies when studying intracellular accumulation of amyloid-beta.

the presence of intracerebral AbetaPP and intracellular Abeta is a normal finding in the developing and aging brain and that intracellular immunoreactive material is not necessarily a sign of pathology.
